meta.titre: Solubility: saturated solutions, tables and crystals on cooling

sections.contenu_markdown: In the Mokolo market in Yaounde, a trader who sells salt knows that a spoonful dissolves quickly in hot soup but a whole handful will leave grains at the bottom of the pot. There is a limit to how much of a substance water can dissolve, and that limit changes with temperature. The same idea is used in industry to make crystals of salt and sugar, and by fish that need dissolved oxygen in the river. In the GCE O/L paper you must define solubility, read values from a table or from a curve, and calculate the mass of crystals that appear when a hot saturated solution cools.

items: A solute dissolves in a solvent to form a solution; water is the most common solvent.
Mass is measured in grams and the mass of a solution is the mass of solute plus the mass of solvent.
Evaporating the water from a solution leaves the dissolved solid behind.

sections.titre: Solubility, saturated solutions and solubility tables
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Solubility** of a substance is the maximum mass of the substance that dissolves in 100 g of water at a stated temperature to form a **saturated solution**. Its unit is **g per 100 g of water**.

- **Unsaturated solution:** can still dissolve more solute at that temperature.
- **Saturated solution:** holds the maximum amount of solute; extra solute stays undissolved.
- **Supersaturated solution:** unstable, holds more than the normal maximum (made by cooling a hot saturated solution carefully); crystals appear if it is disturbed.

A **solubility curve** is a graph of solubility (vertical axis) against temperature (horizontal axis). For most solid salts the solubility rises with temperature, so the curve rises. Points on the curve are saturated; points below the curve are unsaturated.

For salt Y a table gives the solubility at different temperatures:

| Temperature ($^\circ$C) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility of salt Y (g per 100 g of water) | 20 | 25 | 32 | 40 | 50 | 62 |

**Calculations** use proportion, because everything scales with the mass of water:

$$\text{mass of solute that saturates } w \text{ g of water} = \frac{\text{solubility} \times w}{100}$$

A saturated solution made with 100 g of water at 40 $^\circ$C contains 40 g of salt Y, so its mass is $100 + 40 = 140\ \mathrm{g}$.

**Crystals on cooling.** When a saturated solution is cooled, the water can no longer hold the same mass of solute, and the excess forms crystals:

$$\text{mass of crystals} = (\text{solubility at higher temperature} - \text{solubility at lower temperature}) \times \frac{\text{mass of water}}{100}$$

variantes.quand_utiliser: When masses from an evaporation experiment are given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Weigh an empty evaporating dish, add a sample of the saturated solution and weigh again, then evaporate to dryness and weigh once more. Mass of solute = (dish + dry solid) $-$ (empty dish); mass of water = (dish + solution) $-$ (dish + dry solid). Then solubility $= \dfrac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of water}} \times 100$. For example, if the three masses are $20.0\ \mathrm{g}$, $70.0\ \mathrm{g}$ and $30.0\ \mathrm{g}$, the solute is $10.0\ \mathrm{g}$, the water is $40.0\ \mathrm{g}$, and the solubility is $\dfrac{10.0}{40.0} \times 100 = 25\ \mathrm{g}$ per 100 g of water.

variantes.nom: Drawing and reading a solubility curve
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to plot a graph or to read values.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Put temperature on the horizontal axis and solubility on the vertical axis, choose scales that use most of the graph paper, plot each point with a small cross, and draw a **smooth curve** through the points (not a ruler line from point to point). To read a value between two table values, find the temperature on the horizontal axis, go up to the curve, then across to the vertical axis. To find the temperature at which a given mass saturates 100 g of water, start from that mass on the vertical axis and read across and down.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question is about gases or about which salts dissolve.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The solubility of a **gas in water decreases** when the temperature rises, which is why dissolved oxygen is lower in warm rivers and warm drinks go flat. Gas solubility increases when the pressure increases. Useful rules for salts: all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble; all nitrates are soluble; most chlorides are soluble except silver chloride and lead(II) chloride; most sulphates are soluble except barium sulphate and lead(II) sulphate; most carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The solubility of salt Y is given in the table below.

| Temperature ($^\circ$C) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility of salt Y (g per 100 g of water) | 20 | 25 | 32 | 40 | 50 | 62 |

(a) State the solubility of Y at 40 $^\circ$C. (b) What mass of Y is needed to saturate 250 g of water at 40 $^\circ$C, and what is the mass of the solution? (c) The solution is cooled to 20 $^\circ$C. Calculate the mass of crystals that form.

etapes.justification: Solubility is given directly as g per 100 g of water.
250 g is 2.5 times 100 g, so the mass of solute is 2.5 times larger.

etapes.action: Find the mass of the solution.
etapes.justification: Mass of solution = mass of water + mass of solute.
At 20 $^\circ$C the table gives 25 g per 100 g of water, so use 2.5 times that.
Whatever can no longer stay dissolved forms crystals.

sections.conclusion_markdown: A saturated solution made with 250 g of water at 40 $^\circ$C needs $100\ \mathrm{g}$ of Y (solution mass $350\ \mathrm{g}$), and cooling to 20 $^\circ$C gives $37.5\ \mathrm{g}$ of crystals.

items.erreur_markdown: "Solubility is the mass of solute in $100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the solution."
items.pourquoi_faux: Solubility is defined per 100 g of the solvent (water) at a stated temperature, not per volume of solution.
items.correction_markdown: Solubility = mass of solute that saturates 100 g of water at a given temperature.

items.erreur_markdown: "A saturated solution must be a concentrated solution."
items.pourquoi_faux: Saturated, dilute and concentrated describe different things. A substance with very low solubility makes a saturated solution that is still very dilute.
items.correction_markdown: Saturated means no more solute can dissolve at that temperature; concentrated means a lot of solute per volume.

items.erreur_markdown: "The solubility of every solid increases when the temperature rises."
items.pourquoi_faux: This is true for many salts but not all (the solubility of sodium chloride hardly changes), and it is false for gases.
items.correction_markdown: Read the data given; for gases, solubility decreases when temperature rises.

items.erreur_markdown: "A saturated solution made with 100 g of water at 40 $^\circ$C has a mass of 100 g."
items.pourquoi_faux: The 100 g in the definition is the mass of the water. The solution is heavier, $100 + 40 = 140\ \mathrm{g}$.
items.correction_markdown: Always add the dissolved mass to the mass of water to obtain the mass of the solution.

items.erreur_markdown: "I joined the plotted points with a ruler to make a graph."
items.pourquoi_faux: Solubility changes gradually, so the points lie on a smooth curve. Straight segments give wrong values when you read between points.
items.correction_markdown: Draw one smooth curve through (or very close to) all plotted points.

items.enonce_markdown:
Use the solubility table of salt Y.

| Temperature ($^\circ$C) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility of salt Y (g per 100 g of water) | 20 | 25 | 32 | 40 | 50 | 62 |

(a) State the solubility of Y at 50 $^\circ$C. (b) At what temperature does 32 g of Y saturate 100 g of water? (c) 30 g of Y is stirred into 100 g of water at 20 $^\circ$C. What mass dissolves and what mass stays at the bottom?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **50 g** per 100 g of water.

(b) The table shows 32 g at **30 $^\circ$C**.

(c) At 20 $^\circ$C only 25 g can dissolve in 100 g of water, so **25 g dissolves** and $30 - 25 = $ **5 g** stays undissolved. The solution is saturated.

items.enonce_markdown:
A student prepares a saturated solution of salt Y at a certain temperature. An empty evaporating dish has a mass of $20.0\ \mathrm{g}$. After adding some of the saturated solution, the dish and solution have a mass of $48.0\ \mathrm{g}$. The solution is evaporated to dryness and the dish with the dry salt has a mass of $28.0\ \mathrm{g}$.

(a) Calculate the mass of salt and the mass of water in the sample. (b) Calculate the solubility of salt Y at that temperature. (c) Using the table (20 $^\circ$C: 25; 30 $^\circ$C: 32; 40 $^\circ$C: 40; 50 $^\circ$C: 50), find the temperature of the saturated solution.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Salt: $28.0 - 20.0 = $ **8.0 g**. Water: $48.0 - 28.0 = $ **20.0 g**.

(b) Solubility $= \dfrac{8.0}{20.0} \times 100 = $ **40 g per 100 g of water**.

(c) The table gives 40 g per 100 g of water at **40 $^\circ$C**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A saturated solution of salt Y is made at 60 $^\circ$C using 300 g of water. (a) Calculate the mass of Y dissolved and the mass of the solution. (b) The solution is cooled to 30 $^\circ$C. Calculate the mass of crystals formed. (c) Calculate the mass of the solution left above the crystals. (d) Estimate the solubility of Y at 45 $^\circ$C.

| Temperature ($^\circ$C) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility of salt Y (g per 100 g of water) | 20 | 25 | 32 | 40 | 50 | 62 |
items.solution_markdown:
(a) At 60 $^\circ$C: $62 \times 3 = $ **186 g** of Y; solution mass $= 300 + 186 = $ **486 g**.

(b) At 30 $^\circ$C: $32 \times 3 = 96\ \mathrm{g}$ can stay dissolved, so the crystals are $186 - 96 = $ **90 g**.

(c) Solution left: $486 - 90 = $ **396 g** (check: $300 + 96 = 396\ \mathrm{g}$).

(d) The curve is smooth, and 45 $^\circ$C lies half way between 40 $^\circ$C (40 g) and 50 $^\circ$C (50 g), so the solubility is about **45 g per 100 g of water**.

items_markdown: Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of water at a stated temperature to give a saturated solution.
Unsaturated solutions can dissolve more; saturated solutions cannot; supersaturated solutions are unstable.
To scale a table value: mass of solute $=$ solubility $\times$ mass of water $\div$ 100.
Crystals formed on cooling $=$ difference between the solubilities at the two temperatures, scaled to the mass of water.
A solubility curve is drawn as a smooth curve with temperature on the horizontal axis; the solubility of gases falls as temperature rises.
